newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela fishermen lash out over oilspill.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela fishermen lash out over oilspill.

text.p: Venezuelan fishermen on Monday accused tanker owners of trying to avoid responsibility for the pollution caused by an oilspill by the Greek-flagged Nissos Amorgos oil tanker in February.
The accusation was just the latest bout in a war of words over the 25,000 barrel spill in Lake Maracaibo shipping channel which has left the tanker and its captain detained pending legal action.

Tulio Alvarez, a lawyer for the Venezuelan fisherman's union Fetrapesca, said the tanker owners' club Intertanko was trying to blackmail the fishermen with threats of "decertification" of the channel, used for about 70 percent of Venezuela's oil exports.
But an Intertanko spokesman in London said: "Intertanko has neither the mandate nor the ability to decertify the channel," adding that it was not clear what local reports meant by "decertification".
Intertanko director Dagfinn Lunde said last week that Venezuela's detention of the Nissos Amorgos and its captain violated international treaties to which Venezuela was signatory.

He said a bank guarantee for $7.2 million had been provided by a Venezuelan bank on behalf of the Gard P&I Club, the shipowner's insurers, and local indications suggested the clean- up would not exceed this sum. However, the Venezuelan authorities demanded a bond of $46 million to cover claims, interest and other charges, which Intertanko said was unacceptable.
According to treaties to which Venezuela is signatory, any costs above $7.2 million up to a total of 60 million SDR ($81.6 million) are payable by the International Oil Pollution Compensation Fund.

An official from the International Tanker Owners Pollution Fund said in early April that the total clean-up cost up until then was $1-2 million, but a Venezuelan newspaper reported on Monday that they could reach $135 million.
Two claims offices, one in Maracaibo and one in Caracas, had been opened to receive damages claims from anyone affected by the spill, sources added.
Three tankers have grounded seriously in the channel so far this year, causing the port captain to reduce the permitted draught from 39.5 to 36 foot at high tide.
Shipping sources say Venezuela is losing about 150,000 barrels per day in oil exports because of the reduced draught.
